title: Semantic Memory Hierarchies
description_html:
Semantic Memory Hierarchies introduces a governed storage architecture for separating computational memory from durable semantic memory. The paper argues that modern software systems often overload databases by treating transactional state, archives, audit trails, semantic lineage, media records, legal memory, and institutional history as equivalent storage categories. This flattening produces database bloat, hot-path degradation, migration fragility, backup complexity, and epistemic opacity.

The proposed architecture divides system memory into four governed thermal tiers: HOT computational memory, WARM indexed nearby archival memory, COLD canonical immutable archive, and DEEP compressed or offsite preservation. Databases remain bounded hot working memory for active computation, while canonical authority resides in hash-verified, append-only archival structures. Movement between tiers occurs through explicit governed operations such as archive hydration, eviction, demotion, and storage-tier transition receipts.

SMH does not replace databases. It restores them to their strongest role: fast, bounded, transactional computation. Archives become durable, inspectable, portable, semantically authoritative memory. The paper formalizes thermal state, projection discipline, canonical archive authority, rebuildable indexes, advantage boundaries, and interoperability with broader constitutional computing frameworks. Its central contribution is a theory of memory roles for computational systems: hot databases compute, cold archives remember, and governed transitions preserve semantic continuity between them.
